Implement Task 16b ("Loupe reel, corrections from the first real render") from docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-product.md.

Read first: that plan's Task 16 and Task 16b in full; the Global Constraints of docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-core.md; Task 6 of the core plan (the renderer you are restyling); and the current code in packages/reel/src. If the remotion-best-practices and frontend-design skills are available, use them.

Task 16 is implemented and merged; this task corrects four things seen when the scenes were rendered from real data. The reference frames at /Users/yehor/Desktop/projects/neathack-internal/finalists/03-loupe/ (frames.html, frame-1.png to frame-7.png) remain the visual target; read only inside that directory. Docs for the scenes are in docs/design.md.

Item 4 is a performance task with a hard condition: the frames must look the same afterwards. Measure first, change one thing at a time, and keep the before and after stills.

Rendering on this machine needs the environment variable DAILIES_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE, which is already set for you; do not unset it.

This session ends the moment you stop responding, and anything still running in the background is killed. Run renders in the foreground and wait for them. Commit everything before your final report.

There is no `.env` and there are no API keys in this checkout, by design. Rendering needs the network for fonts and a browser download; that is expected.

Commit after each green test cycle. Finish by running the reel package's tests and `pnpm typecheck` at the repo root.

End with a short report: what exists now, test counts, which frames you consider weakest and why, and every deviation from the plan with the reason.

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

10	
11	As of 2026-10-12, `@dailies/reel`'s real renderer (`renderReel`, `renderStills`, and anything that calls them — the pipeline's render stage, the CLI's `dailies run`) fails with:
12	
13	```
14	A delayRender() "Waiting for root component to load - ..." was called but not cleared after 28000ms.
15	```
16	
17	This reproduces on `packages/reel/test/render.test.ts` completely unmodified — it is an environment issue, not a regression from whatever you're working on. Confirm it's still happening before assuming your own code is at fault; don't re-diagnose from scratch.
18	
19	What was ruled out (Task 10 session, ~20 min of diagnosis):
20	- The `chrome-headless-shell` binary itself runs fine standalone (`--version` works; `codesign`/`spctl`/quarantine are clean, gatekeeper blocks LaunchServices-initiated launches, not direct `execve`).
21	- `@remotion/bundler`'s `bundle()` succeeds and serves the bundle (confirmed via an isolated script hitting `bundle()` → `ensureBrowser()` → `openBrowser('chrome')` → `selectComposition()` directly, bypassing `renderReel`).
22	- `openBrowser('chrome')` succeeds (CDP connection works).
23	- The hang is specifically inside Remotion's own in-page root-component-loading JS, after navigation, which never calls `continueRender()`. Not a sandbox/network-isolation issue (reproduces identically with `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true` on the Bash tool).
24	- Not a version mismatch (`remotion`/`@remotion/*` all resolve to 4.0.534, unaffected by an unrelated `pnpm install`).
25	- Not obviously a resource-contention/load issue: failure is deterministic at ~28s every time, including when system load was low; this machine runs many concurrent Claude sessions and their own stray `chrome-headless-shell` processes (check `ps aux | grep headless-shell` — a stuck one from a different worktree was seen, harmless, don't kill another session's processes).
26	
27	Not ruled out / not pursued: Remotion's bundle.js content itself (the actual root-component-loading code in the built player bundle) for a V8/Chromium-157-specific incompatibility. Reel's `package.json` pins `remotion`/`@remotion/*` to `"latest"`, so a routine `pnpm install` can silently bump the whole Remotion/Chromium stack; if this starts passing or failing differently later, that's the first thing to check (`git diff` on `pnpm-lock.yaml` for `remotion`/`@remotion` entries).
28	
29	What still works fine without the real renderer: the full pipeline up through `voice` (ingest → edit → verify → script → ground → voice) runs correctly with a mock model client; only the final `render` stage (and anything downstream of it, like `review`'s stills) is blocked. Mock-model pipeline tests that stop before render are reliable signal.
30	
31	Unrelated: regular Google Chrome over CDP for web screenshots (see [ui-screenshots-headless-chrome](ui-screenshots-headless-chrome.md)) works fine in this same environment — this is specific to Remotion's own bundled renderer, not headless Chrome in general.

As of 2026-10-12, `@dailies/reel`'s real renderer (`renderReel`, `renderStills`, and anything that calls them — the pipeline's render stage, the CLI's `dailies run`) fails with:

```
A delayRender() "Waiting for root component to load - ..." was called but not cleared after 28000ms.
```

This reproduces on `packages/reel/test/render.test.ts` completely unmodified — it is an environment issue, not a regression from whatever you're working on. Confirm it's still happening before assuming your own code is at fault; don't re-diagnose from scratch.

What was ruled out (Task 10 session, ~20 min of diagnosis):
- The `chrome-headless-shell` binary itself runs fine standalone (`--version` works; `codesign`/`spctl`/quarantine are clean, gatekeeper blocks LaunchServices-initiated launches, not direct `execve`).
- `@remotion/bundler`'s `bundle()` succeeds and serves the bundle (confirmed via an isolated script hitting `bundle()` → `ensureBrowser()` → `openBrowser('chrome')` → `selectComposition()` directly, bypassing `renderReel`).
- `openBrowser('chrome')` succeeds (CDP connection works).
- The hang is specifically inside Remotion's own in-page root-component-loading JS, after navigation, which never calls `continueRender()`. Not a sandbox/network-isolation issue (reproduces identically with `dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true` on the Bash tool).
- Not a version mismatch (`remotion`/`@remotion/*` all resolve to 4.0.534, unaffected by an unrelated `pnpm install`).
- Not obviously a resource-contention/load issue: failure is deterministic at ~28s every time, including when system load was low; this machine runs many concurrent Claude sessions and their own stray `chrome-headless-shell` processes (check `ps aux | grep headless-shell` — a stuck one from a different worktree was seen, harmless, don't kill another session's processes).

Not ruled out / not pursued: Remotion's bundle.js content itself (the actual root-component-loading code in the built player bundle) for a V8/Chromium-157-specific incompatibility. Reel's `package.json` pins `remotion`/`@remotion/*` to `"latest"`, so a routine `pnpm install` can silently bump the whole Remotion/Chromium stack; if this starts passing or failing differently later, that's the first thing to check (`git diff` on `pnpm-lock.yaml` for `remotion`/`@remotion` entries).

What still works fine without the real renderer: the full pipeline up through `voice` (ingest → edit → verify → script → ground → voice) runs correctly with a mock model client; only the final `render` stage (and anything downstream of it, like `review`'s stills) is blocked. Mock-model pipeline tests that stop before render are reliable signal.

Unrelated: regular Google Chrome over CDP for web screenshots (see [ui-screenshots-headless-chrome](ui-screenshots-headless-chrome.md)) works fine in this same environment — this is specific to Remotion's own bundled renderer, not headless Chrome in general.

12	
13	- The Playwright MCP tools (`mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__*`) were denied by the permission mode. What worked instead: Google Chrome at `/Applications/Google Chrome.app` started with `--headless=new --remote-debugging-port=<n>` and driven over CDP from a small Node script (Node 24 has a global `WebSocket`): `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, `Page.navigate`, `Runtime.evaluate`, `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` for Tab, `Page.captureScreenshot` with `captureBeyondViewport`.
14	- Open the dev server as `http://localhost:<port>`, not `127.0.0.1`. Next 16 dev blocks cross-origin requests to `/_next/*`, so on `127.0.0.1` the page renders but never hydrates (no effects, no clicks) and nothing in the page says why; the dev log does.
15	- Check CSS in a production build (`next build` + `next start`) too. CSS-module order differs between dev and production, so an override of equal specificity across two modules can win in dev and lose in production.
16	- Never delete `dailies.db` while the server runs: `getDb()` caches the open handle, and the server keeps reading the deleted file. Re-run the seed script instead (it clears the tables), or restart the server.
17	- `next dev` writes an untracked `apps/web/AGENTS.md` on every start.
18	
19	Seed data for the pages: `pnpm --filter @dailies/web exec tsx test/ui/seed.ts <dataDir> [--frames <dir>]`, then start the app with `DAILIES_DATA_DIR=<dataDir>`.

name: ui-screenshots-headless-chrome
description: "How to screenshot the Dailies web app in a non-interactive session, and three traps met doing it"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: b4c27fef-5919-4866-8c3a-b6a85a8e07e9
  modified: 2026-10-11T23:28:19.458Z
---

Screenshots of `apps/web` in a headless (non-interactive) session, as of 2026-10-12:

- The Playwright MCP tools (`mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__*`) were denied by the permission mode. What worked instead: Google Chrome at `/Applications/Google Chrome.app` started with `--headless=new --remote-debugging-port=<n>` and driven over CDP from a small Node script (Node 24 has a global `WebSocket`): `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, `Page.navigate`, `Runtime.evaluate`, `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` for Tab, `Page.captureScreenshot` with `captureBeyondViewport`.
- Open the dev server as `http://localhost:<port>`, not `127.0.0.1`. Next 16 dev blocks cross-origin requests to `/_next/*`, so on `127.0.0.1` the page renders but never hydrates (no effects, no clicks) and nothing in the page says why; the dev log does.
- Check CSS in a production build (`next build` + `next start`) too. CSS-module order differs between dev and production, so an override of equal specificity across two modules can win in dev and lose in production.
- Never delete `dailies.db` while the server runs: `getDb()` caches the open handle, and the server keeps reading the deleted file. Re-run the seed script instead (it clears the tables), or restart the server.
- `next dev` writes an untracked `apps/web/AGENTS.md` on every start.

Seed data for the pages: `pnpm --filter @dailies/web exec tsx test/ui/seed.ts <dataDir> [--frames <dir>]`, then start the app with `DAILIES_DATA_DIR=<dataDir>`.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Dailies Product Layer Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Put the core pipeline behind a web API with a background worker, measure the verifier on real data, and let the agent read its own trace history at run time.

**Architecture:** `apps/web` is a Next.js app that only reads and writes SQLite rows and serves files. A separate worker process executes runs with the durable runner. `eval/` holds benchmarks that reuse `@dailies/ingest` and `@dailies/verify` unchanged. `@dailies/agent` gains a small client for the neatlogs MCP endpoint.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js (App Router, route handlers), better-sqlite3, the packages from the core plan, vitest.

**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md` (sections 5, 6, 7, 9). Builds on `docs/plans/2026-10-11-dailies-core.md`; its Global Constraints apply here unchanged.

## Global Constraints

- Everything in the core plan's Global Constraints.
- The web app never imports `@dailies/reel`, `@remotion/*`, `openai` or `neatlogs`. Rendering and model calls happen only in the worker.
- The worker runs one pipeline at a time.
- No API key is needed to run any test in this plan. Live checks are separate scripts that exit with a clear message when a key is missing.
- Evaluation results never name a repository. Repositories are identified by the first 8 hex characters of the SHA-256 of their URL.

## Review Focus

1. Two requests create runs for the same repository at once: both are accepted and executed one after the other; neither corrupts the other's artifacts. Pinned in Task 11.
2. A client disconnects from the event stream mid-run: the server stops polling for it and the run is unaffected. Pinned in Task 11.
3. A request asks for `/media/<run>/../../.env`: rejected with 400 before touching the filesystem. Pinned in Task 11.
4. A real test-runner output the parser has never seen: counted as `unknown` in the recognition rate, never as a pass. Pinned in Task 12.
5. The neatlogs endpoint is down or returns a non-JSON body: the run proceeds without history and records `memory: skipped`. Pinned in Task 13.

## Task order

Tasks 11, 12 and 13 are independent of each other and of core Tasks 8 and 9. Task 11 needs core Task 7 merged; Task 12 needs core Tasks 2 and 4; Task 13 needs core Task 3. Task 14 needs Task 11 and the chosen visual direction.

1	// The whole art direction of the reel: "Loupe". A strip of film on a switched-off lightbox, a loupe moving
2	// along it, verdicts in grease pencil. Scenes take every colour, family, size, radius and timing from here
3	// and carry none of their own, so a redesign is an edit to this file. docs/design.md describes the direction.
4	import { loadFont as loadDisplay } from '@remotion/google-fonts/Unbounded';
5	import { loadFont as loadText } from '@remotion/google-fonts/Figtree';
6	import { loadFont as loadTextWide } from '@remotion/google-fonts/Manrope';
7	import { loadFont as loadCode } from '@remotion/google-fonts/MartianMono';
8	
9	// Rendering waits for these. Outside a browser (tests, the Node side of the renderer) loadFont does nothing.

1	# Dailies design reference: Loupe
2	
3	The night's work is a strip of film lying on a switched-off lightbox. A loupe moves along it.
4	What sits under the glass is what the narrator is talking about, and the only lit thing in the
5	room is the frame that matters.
6	
7	The anchor is a photo editor's 4× illuminated loupe on 35 mm stock, and the contact-sheet habit
8	of marking selects in grease pencil. Everything below follows from those two objects.
9	
10	The reel renderer (`packages/reel`) is the first implementation. Its tokens live in
11	`packages/reel/src/theme.ts`; nothing under `src/remotion` carries a colour, a size or a family
12	of its own.
13	
14	## Colour
15	
16	| Token | Value | Use |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `lightbox.far` | `#0d1211` | the room, far from the lens |
19	| `lightbox.glass` | `#121917` | the lightbox surface |
20	| `lightbox.near` | `#1a2421` | light spilling around the lens |
21	| `film.base` | `#070a09` | unexposed film between and around frames |
22	| `film.frame` | `#131c19` | a frame's picture area, unlit |
23	| `film.perf` | `#1c2724` | the lightbox seen through a perforation |
24	| `film.lit` | `#2a3f38` | the picture area under the glass |
25	| `white` | `#eef3f1` | type and lit detail |

# Dailies design reference: Loupe

The night's work is a strip of film lying on a switched-off lightbox. A loupe moves along it.
What sits under the glass is what the narrator is talking about, and the only lit thing in the
room is the frame that matters.

The anchor is a photo editor's 4× illuminated loupe on 35 mm stock, and the contact-sheet habit
of marking selects in grease pencil. Everything below follows from those two objects.

The reel renderer (`packages/reel`) is the first implementation. Its tokens live in
`packages/reel/src/theme.ts`; nothing under `src/remotion` carries a colour, a size or a family
of its own.

## Colour

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `lightbox.far` | `#0d1211` | the room, far from the lens |
| `lightbox.glass` | `#121917` | the lightbox surface |
| `lightbox.near` | `#1a2421` | light spilling around the lens |
| `film.base` | `#070a09` | unexposed film between and around frames |
| `film.frame` | `#131c19` | a frame's picture area, unlit |
| `film.perf` | `#1c2724` | the lightbox seen through a perforation |
| `film.lit` | `#2a3f38` | the picture area under the glass |
| `white` | `#eef3f1` | type and lit detail |
| `soft` | `#c3cfca` | secondary type |
| `muted` | `#8fa099` | tertiary type |
| `pencil` | `#ffd60a` | grease pencil, and the verdict pill |
| `ink` | `#0d1211` | type on pencil yellow |

The surface runs from `#0d1211` to `#1a2421`. Yellow is the only accent and it means a verdict.
Added and removed lines in a patch are told apart by weight and brightness, not by hue.

The far field is darker than the black threshold of `ffmpeg blackdetect`, which the review stage
runs. A frame still never reads as black, because the lit glass is in every frame and covers far
more than the two percent of pixels that check needs. `theme.test.ts` pins the luma of `film.lit`
and the smallest share of the frame the glass may cover.

## Type

| Role | Family | Weights | Floor at 1920×1080 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Display | Unbounded | 300, 600, 800 | 72 px |
| Text | Figtree (Manrope for Cyrillic and Greek, which Figtree lacks) | 500, 600 | 40 px |
| Code | Martian Mono | 400, 500 | 30 px |

Display is for the thing a frame is about: a repo name, a figure, a short quote. Text is for
labels, long quotes and captions. Code is for commands, patches and source references.

All faces are loaded through `@remotion/google-fonts`. That package ships Martian Mono at its
normal width only, so code is set at 30 to 32 px, where a column is as wide as in the mock-ups'
condensed 35 px.

Sizes are fitted to measured glyph widths, between the largest size the composition allows and
the floor of the role. Nothing is set below its floor. A word is never broken in two while a
smaller size would keep it whole. A string that cannot fit its frame at the display floor is set
in the text face instead of being cut; only when that fails too is it shortened with an
ellipsis.

Two things are texture and not text, and are exempt from the floors: the film's edge print
(`DAILIES SAFETY FILM`, frame numbers) and the lettering engraved on the loupe's rim. They are
there to be recognised, not read.

## Space, radius, stroke

Spacing scale, in px: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 72, 112.

Radii: pills and the loupe are fully round; the caption bar is 20 px; a frame's picture area and
the perforations are rounded in proportion to the film (about 1 % of the frame pitch).

The whole strip is tilted two degrees anticlockwise, and so is everything seen through the glass.

## The film strip

A horizontal strip of 35 mm stock: a dark base, a row of rounded perforations along each edge, a
hairline of light on both edges, and picture frames. A full frame is eight perforations long and
landscape; a half-frame is four perforations long and portrait. Each scene's content lives on
frames of the strip.

The strip is one continuous object for the whole reel. A scene frames a stretch of it at its own
magnification, so moving to the next scene is a camera move along the film, not a cut: the strip
advances and scales, the perforations stay in phase. The film always moves the same way,
forwards. While it moves fast its perforations and frames are drawn out along their travel, the
way a shutter would smear them. While a scene plays the picture drifts slowly along the strip.

Frames that carry nothing for the current scene hold greeked content: a few soft bars.

## The loupe

One lens, drawn by one component (`Loupe.tsx`): a clear skirt that refracts the film beneath it,
a knurled barrel, a rim engraved `DAILIES OPTICAL 4× ILLUMINATED LOUPE`, glass with a soft
highlight, and a shadow on the lightbox.

The loupe is a persistent layer of the composition and belongs to no scene. Each scene declares
where the lens rests, how large it is and how the barrel is turned (`lens.ts`). Between scenes
the lens glides from one resting place to the next on a spring; the move starts a little before
the cut, is half way at the cut and lands after it. What is under the glass is shown enlarged,
and it slides through the glass faster than the lens travels, the way a real loupe passes over
print. In between two scenes the glass shows the film itself going by, lit; the next scene's
content comes into focus as the lens lands.

Text never touches the rim: content is fitted to the chord of the glass at the height of each
line, less a margin.

## Pencil grammar

Four marks, drawn in yellow grease pencil with a wobbling, waxy stroke. They are used everywhere
and nothing else carries these meanings.

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| a closed ring | verified |
| a cross | contradicted |
| a dashed ring | stale |
| a question mark | unverified |

A mark draws on, as a stroke, while the line it belongs to is spoken: a little way into the
line, once the eye has had time to read what is being marked. Marks pass behind type, which
keeps a halo of the frame's colour, so a crossed-out quote stays readable. A ring is sized to
clear the ends of the letters it goes round.

The verdict of a flagged claim is also set in words on a yellow pill.

## Scenes

**Title.** The lens rests on the repo name, set in display inside the glass; a name too long for
one line puts its owner above it in the text face. The window label is set large beside it, with
the session and commit counts under it and the wordmark in the corner. The strip passes behind
with greeked frames. The reel opens with the film being pulled into place under a lens that is
already waiting.

**Prompt.** The lens grows until the glass fills the frame. Through it: `You asked`, the human's
request, and its session reference in code. A short request is set in display; a long one in the
text face.

**Terminal.** One frame per step. A frame carries the command, the decisive part of its output
set large (`2 failed`, `14 passed`), the rest of the result under it, and its source reference.
Output with no count in it gives its last line, in code. The lens holds still while the strip
advances a frame at a time, so the step being spoken is the one under the glass and the steps
already told sit to its left. A passing step is ringed; a failing step is crossed. The scene
comes to rest on the last step. A scene with a single step has a larger lens in the middle of
the frame.

**Diff.** The largest lens. Through it: the file name in display with its directory in code, the
added and removed counts, and the patch in code. Added lines sit on a faint band of light at
full strength; removed lines are dimmed. When the patch is longer than the glass, the window
with the most changed lines is shown and the rest is counted.

**Stats.** One half-frame per value, the figure in display over its label. The lens rests at the
head of the strip on the first value and shows it enlarged; the others follow from where its
skirt ends, at a pitch that keeps all of them in the frame and at one size. Figures count up as
the lens lands.

**Flag.** On the left, a frame with the agent's quote under `the agent said` and the pencil
through it: a cross for a contradicted claim, a dashed ring around a stale one. Beside it the
lens rests on the recorded reality, which is ringed; when the record ends on a count, the count
is set in display and the ring goes round it alone. A long record gets a larger glass. The
verdict sits across the foot of the lens on a yellow pill, `CONTRADICTED` or `STALE`, stamped
down after the pencil, and the source reference is printed on the film's edge under the quote.

**End.** The repo name; a strip of small frames with one mark per claim, rings for verified,
crosses for flagged, question marks for unverified, in that order, at most 16 with `+n` after
them; under it the three counts in words, a count of zero dimmed. When more than 16 claims were
checked the 16 marks keep the proportions of the three kinds and never drop a kind that
occurred. The lens rests at the end of the strip over the wordmark.

## Captions

A captions-only cut shows the line being spoken in a bar at the bottom of the frame: film-base
black, 20 px radius, text face, up to three lines. Every narrated scene moves up to keep that
inset clear. A voiced cut has no bar and uses the full frame.

## Motion

- The lens glide and the film advance between scenes share one spring. It follows a short ramp,
  so the lens leaves softly, and it settles with a trace of overshoot.
- The strip advances a frame at a time inside the terminal scene.
- Pencil marks draw on with their line; the verdict pill stamps down after its mark.
- Figures count up; content under the glass pulls into focus.
- Everything except the marks and the terminal's steps has landed before the middle of its scene.

Review stills are taken at the middle of each scene, as the captions cut, with every mark and
every step already landed, so a still shows all a scene will hold.
